slides: Sentence structure and punctuation.
So, the language rubric asks for varied sentence structures. Let's see what that means in practice, and how punctuation helps.
First, sentence structures. There are all kinds of sentence types, but we don't want to get into that.
We don't care about the terms. This isn't a grammar exam.
So what does it mean in practice? Your sentences shouldn't all be short. And they shouldn't be heavy and overloaded either.

You don't need to think about it too much, or try to build different structures on purpose. Just write naturally, and let it flow. Where a sentence needs splitting, split it, and use punctuation to do that.
Let's look at an example. One problem students have is sentences that are too short. It breaks the flow of reading.
If a whole paragraph looks like this... full stop, full stop, full stop... it ruins the flow. You can't really read it.
So what do we do? We join some of these sentences together.
For example, identify suspicious activity before an offence, comma, stop it while it happens, comma, or catch offenders afterwards.
So I joined three sentences into one, and I got a varied sentence structure.
Now the other extreme. An overloaded sentence.
Sorry... I'm out of breath.
One sentence, a million commas, lots of parts. Why? Well, that's the other extreme. Not short sentences, but one sentence with so many parts that we stop breathing.
With so many connecting words, one after the other, you don't remember anymore how the parts of the sentence connect to each other.
A good sentence is one you can read in one breath. So take one breath, and if you manage to finish the sentence, that's a sign it's fine.
If you don't make it, that's a warning sign. It might be too long.
And variety isn't something you build on purpose. It comes naturally, once you join some sentences and split others.
Now let's see this paragraph written properly, and comfortably.
Full stop after the first sentence. Pause. Breathe.
Each time, I took a few sentences and joined them. And the result is varied sentence structure.
You don't need to push. It comes naturally once you join sentences. Just don't do what I did before. Sentences that are too short, or one long, overloaded sentence.
Now, punctuation. There are lots of punctuation marks, and all kinds of rules. And again, we don't want to get into all of it.
So what do we want from punctuation? Its job is to make the reader read the essay the way I'd want to read it to them.
The reader is like a puppet on strings. I tell them when to stop, what to stress... I can even change their tone while they read.
We won't go through every mark, only the main ones. Honestly, for the exam, the full stop and the comma are almost enough. But it's good to know the others, so you see when you might need them.
The full stop. At the end of every sentence, anywhere the reading stops. Did you notice? I stopped. There's a full stop there.
The comma. Wherever there should be a short pause in the reading... but not a full stop like a period.
Did you see what I did there? A short pause, comma, but not a full stop.
Now, in English, one of the most useful comma rules is this. Put a comma after an opening phrase. 'In recent years, comma'. 'On the other hand, comma'. 'If the law passes, comma'.

And before 'and' or 'but' when it joins two full sentences, each with its own subject. 'Cameras may deter crime, comma, and they can help the police'. But in a simple list, like 'cameras and sensors', there's no comma.
And the most important rule, I think. When you want the reader to pause for a moment, put a comma.
There's one thing a comma can't do in English. It can't join two full sentences on its own.
Two complete sentences, with only a comma between them. That's called a comma splice, and it's one of the most common mistakes in English essays.
So, a full stop. A semicolon. Or a comma plus a connecting word, like 'and' or 'but'.
And watch out for 'however'. It's not like 'but'. Between two full sentences, it needs a full stop or a semicolon before it, and a comma after it.
The semicolon joins two full sentences that are closely connected. We just saw it.
The colon. We use it in the following cases.
One, a list of details. What was on the table: a plate, comma, a fork, comma, a glass, and so on.
Two, when I quote, or there's direct speech.
Three, when an explanation comes next. Like right here... 'in the following cases', colon.
The dash. It's a stronger separation, often before an explanation, like a colon. This regulation is a dead letter, dash, nobody actually follows it.
Brackets. They're for an addition, or a side note. For example, when you define an abbreviation.
Quotation marks. For a quote, a name, a term you're talking about, or, rarely, an informal word you use on purpose.
And by the way, 'a dead letter' is a great expression for the essay. It means a rule that exists on paper, but nobody follows.
The question mark goes only after a direct question. 'The question is whether' is indirect, so no question mark. And no rhetorical questions in the essay.
The exclamation mark is for an order, or strong emotion. Not for academic writing.
So, can we use all these marks in academic writing? Here's the summary.
Quotation marks. Allowed when you need them, when they serve the content.
Abbreviations. Usually we don't use them, unless we defined them earlier.
Brackets. Allowed, but it's better to try to say it without them. If something is important, write it, with commas, not in brackets.
The exclamation mark. Basically, no. It's very strong, like a shout. That kind of emphasis doesn't fit academic writing.
Etcetera. Better not. Write it out. 'And similar measures', 'and other public services'.
Three dots. Better not, and that's also about content. We said nothing is obvious. Three dots means 'you figure it out'. And we want to explain.
And one that's special to English. No contractions.
